To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
during long duration flight pigeons' pairwise distances and group level distances increase, while flap frequency decreases.
during a long-duration flight, pigeons flew in a more dispersed cluster flock, which was characterized by a reduction in flap frequency.
Cluster flocking is costly, particularly in dense flocks.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how animals make trade offs between different functions and how these trade offs change over time and space.
how animals make decisions in a changing environment.
understanding how the proximate mechanisms of cluster flocking are influenced by the ultimate function of flocking, which in turn can influence how birds use the environment.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
cluster flocks of pigeons can provide a useful system for studying the trade offs between group level benefits and individual level costs of flocking.

during long duration flight in cluster flocks, birds reduce their flap frequency, and therefore work rate, to avoid flying in close proximity to conspecifics, and that these changes in flap rate and flock structure occur as a result of fatigue.
the benefits of flocking (predator deterrence) are overridden by the costs (increased energetic expenditure).
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
cluster flocking is costly and that the costs of flying close outweigh the anti-predatory benefits.
the benefits of flocking may not outweigh the costs of flying in dense clusters over long durations.
during short duration flights (less than 1 hr) the benefits of flocking (e.g. anti-predator, thermoregulation, navigation, foraging) are greater than the energetic costs of close proximity.
The main takeaway from our work is that
birds may use cluster flocking as a means to reduce the cost of flight, and not just as a means to avoid predators.
the costs and benefits of flocking are dynamic and can change over time.
cluster flocking is not always the most energetically efficient flight strategy.
